The grammar of plots

A plot is a sentence with a few parts: the data, the mappings from columns to channels, the layers that draw them, the scales that turn data into positions and colors, the facets that split it into panels, and the theme. Each part is one method. Each method returns a new plot.

01

Data

A plot starts with a table in long format: one row per observation, one column per variable. Here each row is one value of one indicator, measured by one sensor at one time. Wide tables (one column per sensor) become long with pandas melt().

return week.head(6)
time sensor indicator value
2026-10-13 00:00:00 sensor A UV254 (1/m) 3.5758
2026-10-13 00:15:00 sensor A UV254 (1/m) 3.5740
2026-10-13 00:30:00 sensor A UV254 (1/m) 3.5044
2026-10-13 00:45:00 sensor A UV254 (1/m) 3.4334
2026-10-13 01:00:00 sensor A UV254 (1/m) 3.4488
2026-10-13 01:15:00 sensor A UV254 (1/m) 3.3885
02

Mappings

plot() takes the data and maps columns to channels: x, y, color, group, tooltip, label, ... A mapping alone draws nothing. A layer draws it: here, point().

p = plot(one, x="time", y="value").point()
03

Layers

Layers stack in the order you add them. Each layer uses the plot mappings for its channels. Here: a line, then the points on top, then a reference line.

p = plot(one, x="time", y="value").line().point(size=2.5).hline(y=4)
04

Mapping or setting

A string that names a column is a mapping: the color then changes with the data, and a legend shows. Any other value is a setting: one color (a theme color or a CSS color), one size, one line pattern.

mapped = plot(day, x="time", y="value", color="sensor").line()
setting = plot(one, x="time", y="value").line(color="red", size=3, dash="dashed")
return [mapped, setting]
05

Layer data

A layer can have its own data with data=. hline, vline, abline and band do not use the plot mappings, so a reference line needs only its own value.

events = pd.DataFrame({"time": pd.to_datetime(["2026-10-15 06:00", "2026-10-15 18:30"]), "event": ["filter", "cleaning"]})
p = (
    plot(day, x="time", y="value", color="sensor")
    .line()
    .vline(data=events, x="time", color="gray", dash="dotted")
    .text(data=events, x="time", y=7.4, label="event")
)
06

Statistics

Some layers compute before they draw: hist counts in bins, density smooths a distribution, smooth fits a trend, box computes quartiles, and summary= reduces the rows at each x.

hist = plot(week[week.indicator == "turbidity (NTU)"], x="value", color="sensor").hist(bins=30, position="overlay")
trend = plot(uv, x="time", y="value", color="sensor").point(size=1, alpha=0.3).smooth(method="loess", span=0.3)
return [hist, trend]
07

Position

position= says how the bars of one x share the space: stack (the default) adds them up, dodge puts them side by side, overlay draws them over each other.

spring = monthly[monthly.month_name.isin(["Mar", "Apr", "May"])]
return [
    plot(spring, x="month_name", y="volume", color="site").bar(position=pos).labels(title=f'position="{pos}"').theme(height=240)
    for pos in ("stack", "dodge", "overlay")
]
08

Position scales

Scales turn data into positions and colors. x() and y() set the type (linear, log, time, category), the limits of the first view (None keeps the data bound) and the label format.

p = (
    plot(uv, x="time", y="value", color="sensor")
    .line()
    .x(limits=[pd.Timestamp("2026-10-14"), pd.Timestamp("2026-10-16")], format="%a %H:%M")
    .y(limits=[0, None])
)
09

Color scales

color() sets the color scale. Categories use a palette (or values=); numbers use a scheme, and a diverging scheme with mid= centers a reference value.

spectra = load("spectra")
categories = plot(uv, x="time", y="value", color="sensor").line().color(palette="momiji")
numbers = plot(spectra, x="wavelength", y="absorbance", color="hour", group="hour").line().color(scheme="ai")
return [categories, numbers]
10

Facets

Facets split the data into panels: facet() by one column, grid() by two. free="y" gives each panel its own y range; shared axes stay aligned.

p = plot(week, x="time", y="value", color="sensor").line(size=1).facet("indicator", free="y", ncol=1).theme(height=520)
11

Labels and themes

labels() sets the titles; None removes one. theme() sets the style (the colors and the font) and the format (the size): screen follows the page width, report and slide have a fixed size.

p = (
    plot(uv, x="time", y="value", color="sensor")
    .line()
    .labels(title="UV254 over one week", subtitle="15-min values", x=None, y="UV254 (1/m)", caption="Made-up data")
    .theme("wota")
)
12

Interaction and output

The same plot is static (with copy and download buttons) or interactive. save() writes a PNG or an SVG with the same look; width= lays the plot out again at that size.

p = plot(uv, x="time", y="value", color="sensor").line()

p                                  # static, at the width of the cell
p.interactive()                    # zoom, pan, hover, legend toggle
p.save("uv.png", width=1600)       # a PNG for slides
p.theme("pastel", format="slide").save("uv_slide.svg")
13

The spec

Under the hood, a plot is a small JSON spec. The Python and the JavaScript builders write the same spec, and one renderer draws it everywhere: in a notebook, on a web page, in a file.

p = plot(day.head(3), x="time", y="value", color="sensor").line().hline(y=5).labels(title="UV254")
return p.spec()
{
 "version": 1,
 "data": [
  {
   "columns": {
    "time": {
     "type": "time",
     "values": [
      1792022400000,
      1792023300000,
      1792024200000
     ]
    },
    "value": {
     "type": "number",
     "values": [
      3.882,
      3.7677,
      3.7986
     ]
    },
    "sensor": {
     "type": "string",
     "values": [
      "sensor A",
      "sensor A",
      "sensor A"
     ]
    }
   }
  }
 ],
 "mapping": {
  "x": "time",
  "y": "value",
  "color": "sensor"
 },
 "layers": [
  {
   "type": "line",
   "mapping": {},
   "set": {}
  },
  {
   "type": "hline",
   "mapping": {},
   "set": {
    "y": 5
   }
  }
 ],
 "facet": null,
 "scales": {},
 "labels": {
  "title": "UV254"
 },
 "theme": {
  "style": "pastel"
 }
}
14

Python and JavaScript

The JavaScript builder has the same methods. Keyword arguments become option objects.

# Python
plot(df, x="time", y="value", color="sensor").line().facet("indicator", free="y")

// JavaScript
plot(rows, { x: "time", y: "value", color: "sensor" }).line().facet("indicator", { free: "y" })

// React
<Plot spec={plot(rows, { x: "time", y: "value" }).line()} interactive />
